lines.text: LOSS OF LIFE FOLLOWING MAN OVERBOARD FROM P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST
06May13
Captain
seemed embarrassed by this discovery, but made no action to punish
or reprimand the transgressors. She noted that crew members frequently broke another
company policy by staying up after midnight. Finally, Captain
openly
permitted crewmembers to utilize the dining room to play video games despite the "Crew
in Quarters after Midnight" policy. She cited that the crew appreciated having the space
to congregate together and that it was good for overall morale. Strict enforcement of
policy by vessel managers sends a message to employees that breaking the rules is not
tolerated. Company rules and policies exist to keep people safe, but without effective
enforcement, the rules will be broken, as evidenced in this investigation. Captain
and other management staff onboard P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST must take
enforcement action against persons who violate safety policies to prevent future
incidents.
3) Barriers: An insufficiency of barriers permitted easy access to the stern by passengers
and crew alike. The only physical barriers were "Employees Only" safety chains placed
on the main deck walkways to prevent passengers from approaching the stern. But on
both Coast Guard visits, investigators found these chains hanging from the bulkhead
instead of stretched across the walkways. Captain
stated that crewmembers
routinely forgot to put these barriers in place. Again, there was no evidence of any
consequences for neglectful crew who didn't replace the chains.
Railings: Two sections on the port side stern near the paddlewheel were missing
effective railings to prevent a person from falling overboard. Mr. Staples fell through the
smaller of the two sections (a 54 inch section). During the cosmetic paddlewheel
installation project, Coast Guard and vessel representatives determined that railings in
these sections were inappropriate due to the heightened chance of river debris becoming
lodged in the railing and damaging vital ship's equipment. The smaller section was left
completely exposed, but the larger of the two sections (the ten-foot section) was supposed
to be equipped with a chain to warn and prevent personnel from approaching the stern.
However, the chain was never fabricated or put in place following the project. The
missing smaller railing must be considered to be a causal factor in this case, but the
installation of a new railing was not advised due to the increased risk of damage to
propulsion equipment.
d) Personnel: There are three personnel factors related to Mr. Andres Staples.
1) Alcohol Consumption: According to gathered evidence and witness statements Mr.
Staples consumed two mixed drinks (Jack and Coke) and one standard bottle of beer (12
oz.) in a one-hour period. A total of three hours and twenty-five minutes passed from
when he signed off the vessel until when he entered the water. Mr. Staples weighed
approximately 200 pounds, according to his driver's license. According to most Blood
Alcohol Content (BAC) charts and calculators, a 200 pound man who consumed the same
amount of alcohol over the same period of time would have a BAC around 0.01%, not
enough to legally impair a person. An individual's blood alcohol concentration depends
on a variety of additional factors, so it is difficult to accurately assess Mr. Staples' actual
levels. Complicating the investigation is the fact that Mr. Staples' whereabouts are
unknown for a period of about forty-five minutes between when he signed back on to the
vessel and when the first witnesses recount seeing him in the dining room. It is possible
that he may have consumed more alcohol on the vessel, but not likely, as alcohol
containers were not found on his person or in his personal effects. Without further
evience or witness testimony that Mr. Staples consumed additional alcohol, his blood
alcohol content cannot be assumed to be at a level to impair him.
